title: Magnetic anisotropy in the near-stoichiometric van der Waals ferromagnet Fe$_3$GeTe$_2$
authors: Riju Pal, Joyal John Abraham, Satyabrata Bera, Mintu Mondal, Atindra Nath Pal, Bernd Buchner, Vladislav Kataev, Alexey Alfonsov
abstract: Quasi-two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) ferromagnets such as the series Fe$_{3-x}$GeTe$_2$, with a relatively high Curie temperature and robust metallicity, offer an ideal platform for investigating itinerant magnetism in reduced dimensions. Here, we present a comprehensive electron spin resonance (ESR) investigation of single-crystalline almost-stoichiometric Fe$_{3.03 \pm 0.03}$GeTe$_{2}$ across wide ranges of frequencies, temperatures, and magnetic fields to gain quantitative insights into its magnetic anisotropy and spin dynamics. Frequency-dependent ESR measurements establish Fe$_{3}$GeTe$_{2}$ as an easy-axis ferromagnet. Temperature-dependent high-field ESR reveals a large internal field that gradually decreases at higher temperatures. Remarkably, this internal field persists even above $T_\mathrm{C}$, evidencing short-range spin correlations in Fe$_{3}$GeTe$_{2}$. Analysis of spin-wave modes yields a strong uniaxial magnetocrystalline anisotropy $K_{\text{int}} \approx - 5 \times 10^6$ erg cm$^{-3}$ at 3 K and a large magnon gap $Δ(3 \mathrm{K})$ $\approx$ 87.8 $\pm$ 13.7 GHz ($\approx$ 0.363 $\pm$ 0.057 meV). Our study highlights that small variations in Fe content in Fe$_{3}$GeTe$_{2}$ lead to substantial changes in the magnon gap at low temperatures, indicating the extreme sensitivity of spin dynamics to the chemical composition. These results establish Fe$_{3}$GeTe$_{2}$ as a model vdW ferromagnet for exploring tunable anisotropies and magnon excitations in metallic 2D magnets.
summary: This work uses high-frequency Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) on $	ext{Fe}_3	ext{GeTe}_2$ to characterize its magnetic anisotropy and spin dynamics. Key findings include confirming easy-axis ferromagnetism, measuring a large magnon gap, and showing that the material's magnetic properties are extremely sensitive to minor changes in chemical stoichiometry. It establishes this compound as an excellent model system for studying tunable magnetism in 2D materials.
main_problem: To gain quantitative insights into the magnetic anisotropy and spin dynamics of quasi-two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals ferromagnets, specifically investigating the role of Fe stoichiometry.
main_result: The study established $	ext{Fe}_3	ext{GeTe}_2$ as an easy-axis ferromagnet with a large magnon gap ($\approx 87.8 	ext{ GHz}$ at $3 	ext{ K}$) and demonstrated that spin dynamics are extremely sensitive to small variations in Fe content.
method: The primary methods involved comprehensive Electron Spin Resonance (ESR) measurements across wide ranges of frequencies, temperatures, and magnetic fields, supplemented by magnetization measurements ($M-T$, $M-H$).
model_or_system: The physical system is the near-stoichiometric van der Waals ferromagnet $	ext{Fe}_3	ext{GeTe}_2$, which exhibits itinerant magnetism in a quasi-two-dimensional layered structure.
key_observables: Magnetic anisotropy, internal magnetic field evolution with temperature, uniaxial magnetocrystalline anisotropy ($K_{	ext{int}}$), and the zero-field magnon gap ($\Delta$).
important_parameters: Low temperatures (e.g., $3 	ext{ K}$), specific stoichiometry variations ($	ext{Fe}_{3.03} 	ext{GeTe}_2$), and high magnetic fields ($16 	ext{ T}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on fitting the experimental data to established models for uniaxial ferromagnets, assuming the material behaves as a model vdW ferromagnet.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate crystal structure details (hexagonal symmetry), temperature dependence of magnetization ($M-T$), and how magnetic anisotropy parameters vary with field orientation relative to the $c$-axis.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first characterizing the material's basic ferromagnetic nature via frequency-dependent ESR, then analyzing the temperature evolution of the internal field to detect short-range correlations above $T_C$, and finally quantifying anisotropy parameters like $K_{	ext{int}}$ and $\Delta$ using spin-wave analysis.
why_interesting: The study provides quantitative measurements of magnon excitations and magnetic anisotropy in a highly tunable 2D system, which is crucial for understanding emergent quantum phenomena in low-dimensional magnets relevant to spintronics and quantum simulation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. (a) Crystal structure of Fe3GeTe2. The unit cell (left) and the top view (right) of a single vdW layer of Fe3GeTe2 are shown here. The unit cell is enclosed using the dotted lines. The top view of the structure shows the hexagonal symmetry of the ab plane. Two inequivalent Fe sites are termed Fe1 and Fe2. (b) The temperature dependence of magnetization and its temperature derivative, measured under a magnetic field of 500 Oe in the H ∥c and H ⊥c configurations. The minimum in the temperature derivative of the magnetization (dM/dT) reveals the Curie temperature TC ∼215 K of Fe3GeTe2.

Figure 2. Frequency dependence of the resonance fields Hres at T = 3 K (a) and 100 K (b) measured in H ∥c (blue squares) and in H ⊥c (red circles) configurations, respectively. Dashed lines represent the paramagnetic response estimated with Eq. 1 with the average g-factors given in the legends. Solid lines indicate the simulated best fit results using Eq. 2.1 and 2.2. Representative normalized and vertically shifted spectra are shown for some of the frequencies (right vertical axis) with the colors following respective magnetic field orientations.

Figure 3. Temperature evolution of the HF-ESR spectra in the field direction H ∥c (a) and H ⊥c (b), measured at fixed excitation frequencies of approximately 300 GHz. For clarity, all spectra are normalized to unity and vertically offset. Vertical black solid lines indicate the expected paramagnetic resonance position as given by Eq. 1. (c) Temperature dependence of the resonance shift, δH(T), at a microwave frequency ν of ≈300 GHz with an external magnetic field applied parallel (blue squares) and perpendicular (red circles) to the c axis. Figure 4. (a) Total anisotropy field Ha as a function of temperature for both H ⊥c and H ∥c configurations, extracted from the temperature dependence of the resonance fields. The purple solid line is the calculated shape anisotropy field HD given by the shape of the crystal. Green stars are the total anisotropy field calculated from the M −H data. (b) Temperature dependence of the intrinsic MA constant (Kint) estimated from the measurements in the H ⊥c and H ∥c configurations, respectively.

Figure 5. Anisotropy energy density demonstration in Carte- sian coordinates (following Eq. 5), illustrating magnetic anisotropy of a single sublattice of Fe3GeTe2, as follows from the analysis of the HF-ESR results. Here, the yellow color corresponds to the energetically favorable direction (easy axis along the c-axis), while blue indicates higher-energy regions (hard plane). The surface is rotationally symmetric about the z-axis, reflecting the uniaxial magnetic anisotropy of the crystal.
